past_actions.summary: Prepare and send a formal internal memo to AutoShield regional leadership documenting the policy collapse — 25 active policies in Millfield, structural shift from personal auto to corporate/fleet liability, and a recommendation that the region pivot toward commercial fleet risk assessment rather than personal auto renewals. This is not a panic signal; it is a proactive positioning move that shows I understand the landscape and am managing it rather than waiting to be managed.

Have the one-on-one with Priya Sharma that she requested — and do it honestly. When she delivers her field assessment that the personal auto book is structurally terminal, I don't deflect. I confirm I share that read. I tell her what I did in tick 4: that I already sent the memo to corporate making the case for a commercial fleet pivot. I tell her I don't have a response yet. I ask her directly: if AutoShield does not pivot, what is her own timeline? I am not telling her to start looking — but I am treating her like an adult who already knows the math. This protects my credibility with her more than any reassurance would.

reflections.reflection: Six months in. The personal auto book is not declining — it is collapsing. We went from 25 active policies to 22 in two ticks, and the trend is not reversing. RoboRide is on the streets, people are selling their cars, unemployment is at 23%, and consumer spending is at half of baseline. The structural shift I documented in my tick 4 memo is visible to everyone on the street now, not just in the data. What I have learned from these three months: acting early matters but it is not sufficient. I sent the corporate memo six ticks ago and heard nothing. I started the CRMP cert which was the right call. I made the external applications but did not follow through on the follow-up calls. Priya and I had an honest conversation that I think preserved my credibility with her, but she is watching her own clock now, which means I cannot rely on team loyalty as a buffer much longer.
reflections.identity_shift: I came into this as a Regional Manager who believed the role itself had stability — that managing risk for others gave me insulation from it. That belief has eroded. I am now thinking of myself less as 'insurance manager' and more as 'risk professional who happens to currently work in personal auto.' That reframe is uncomfortable but it is probably what saves me. My identity attachment to this specific role was already at 0.5 — it is lower now. I do not feel proud of that, but I think it is honest.
regrets: I committed to three follow-up phone calls to external employers after tick 2 and I have not made them. That is six months of leads going cold while I told myself I would get to it.
I should have asked corporate for a response timeline in the original pivot memo — an open-ended memo is easy to ignore.
I have not had a direct conversation with Tom Bradley about his own timeline or what the commercial briefing response actually means. I am relying on word of mouth.
successes: The CRMP certification is in progress and on track. Two months in, 20% complete. This is the one thing I am doing for future-Linda regardless of what AutoShield decides.
The Priya Sharma conversation at tick 5 was honest and credibility-preserving. She knows I am not pretending. That matters.
The tick 4 corporate memo was proactive positioning — even if unanswered, it creates a paper trail that I saw this coming and acted on it.
reflections.adaptation_notes: I am adapting, but slowly and incompletely. I have taken the structural actions — certification, memo, applications — but I have not followed through on the operational ones, specifically the follow-up calls. There is a version of me that is genuinely adapting and a version that is doing the appearance of adapting without closing the loop. This tick I need to be the first version. The phone calls are not optional anymore. Corporate silence is a signal I can no longer treat as neutral.
